issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette:
Marcus Holt is a 34-year-old Navy officer, married, who presented for an initial psychological evaluation following a referral from his unit's medical officer. He carries himself with the composed bearing one might expect from someone who has spent years operating in high-stakes environments, yet there is something effortful about that composure now - a quality of maintenance rather than ease. He is soft-spoken in session, choosing his words carefully, as though he is still not entirely certain that what happened to him is something worth discussing.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Marcus was on approved leave visiting extended family in a coastal community in the Gulf South when a rapidly intensifying hurricane made landfall with little warning. He and several family members, including his wife's younger brother, were sheltering in a single-story home when the storm surge overwhelmed the structure. The water rose faster than anyone had anticipated. In the chaos that followed - darkness, the roar of wind and water, the press of debris - Marcus found himself separated from the others, pinned briefly beneath a collapsed interior wall in chest-high water, unable to determine who was around him or whether anyone was calling out. The smell in the air was a sour, fetid mixture of floodwater and the contents of a nearby liquor cabinet that had shattered in the surge. His wife's brother did not survive. Marcus did, pulled free by a neighbor who had heard him. He has described the hours that followed - waiting in a crowded emergency shelter, pressed against strangers, unable to account for everyone - as worse in some ways than the water itself.

In the weeks after returning to duty, Marcus noticed that his memories of the event did not behave like other memories. They came as images rather than narrative - a flash of dark water, the angle of a ceiling beam, a particular quality of light through a broken window - and when they arrived, he felt his body respond as though it were still pinned: his chest would compress, his arms would brace. What unsettled him most was the sense that the memory felt cinematically extreme, almost impossible to locate in his own biography. He has said more than once, with a kind of bewildered flatness, that it doesn't feel like something that actually happened to him. And yet his body insists otherwise.

He had come to believe, quietly and with some conviction, that he deserved whatever suffering came to him. His reasoning, never fully articulated until recently, was shaped by his survival - by the fact that he, a trained officer, had not been able to do more. This belief has not taken the form of dramatic self-recrimination but of something quieter and more corrosive: a sense that comfort or relief would be somehow dishonest, and that he ought not seek either. He began telling himself this in the shelter, and he has not stopped.

The practical consequences have accumulated over months. Marcus stopped accepting invitations from friends in his unit - dinners, social gatherings - until the invitations stopped coming. His wife has noticed the withdrawal but has interpreted it as grief, which is not entirely wrong. He avoids the commissary during peak hours when it is crowded, routing his errands to early morning slots, and he has begun timing his movements around the base to minimize the press of bodies. He keeps clear of any situation that might replicate the sensory texture of that night: he will not sit in dim rooms, will not enter spaces where he cannot see the exits clearly, and the smell of alcohol - present at any number of officer social functions - has become something he physically removes himself from, sometimes without explanation. His supervisor has noted his absences from unit social events, and there has been an informal conversation about whether Marcus is "still himself."

He has come to feel, with a certainty that surprises him when he examines it, that he no longer belongs anywhere in particular - not fully among his colleagues, not fully at home, not anywhere he inhabited before the storm. He describes himself as standing slightly outside whatever room he is in. What finally brought him to seek help was his wife asking him, plainly and without anger, whether he thought things would ever feel normal again. He did not have an answer. He is most afraid that the answer is no.
